blocks.text: Consider the function \(f : \mathbb{R} \to [-1, 1]\) define by \(f(x) = \cos x\). The graph of the function is shown in Figure 9.4.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "define by"; it should read "defined by": the function \(f : \mathbb{R} \to [-1, 1]\) defined by \(f(x) = \cos x\).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cos x from minus 4 pi to 4 pi. The wave has maximum value 1 at even multiples of pi and minimum value minus 1 at odd multiples of pi; dashed lines y = 1 and y = minus 1 touch it at all these points.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.4: Graph of f(x) = cos x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Like the graph of the sine function, the graph of the cosine function is not bijective because again it fails the horizontal line test. It touches the line \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) at multiple points. However, if we carefully restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \cos x\) to the closed interval \([0, \pi]\), then the function with restricted domain, i.e., \(f : [0, \pi] \to [-1, 1]\), becomes one-one and onto, that is invertible, and is called the principal cosine function. The inverse cosine function is defined by

blocks.text_alt: y equals cosine inverse of x if and only if x equals cosine of y

blocks.text: The domain of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is \([-1, 1]\) and the range of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is \([0, \pi]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why not use \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) again, as for sine? Because cosine is not one-to-one there: \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\). Cosine is an even function, so a negative angle and the matching positive angle always give the same value. Also, on that interval cosine never becomes negative, so it would not be onto \([-1, 1]\).
On \([0, \pi]\), Figure 9.4 shows cosine falling steadily from \(1\) (at \(0\)) to \(-1\) (at \(\pi\)): it takes every value of \([-1, 1]\) exactly once. So the restriction is one-to-one and onto.
Remember the two ranges side by side: \(\sin^{-1}\) gives angles in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) (first and fourth quadrants); \(\cos^{-1}\) gives angles in \([0, \pi]\) (first and second quadrants).

blocks.caption: Domain and range swap places (our summary)

blocks.text: The graph of the function \(\cos : [0, \pi] \to [-1, 1]\) is shown in Figure 9.5(a), and the graph of \(\cos^{-1} : [-1, 1] \to [0, \pi]\) is shown in Figure 9.5(b).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cos x only from 0 to pi. It falls steadily from the point (0, 1), crosses the x-axis at pi over 2, and ends at the point (pi, minus 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 9.5(a): Graph of y = cos x from 0 to π (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse cosine of x from minus 1 to 1. It falls from the point (minus 1, pi), crosses the y-axis at pi over 2, and ends at the point (1, 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 9.5(b): Graph of y = cos⁻¹ x from −1 to 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The points swap again: \((0, 1)\) and \((\pi, -1)\) on the cosine graph become \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, \pi)\) on the inverse cosine graph. The \(x\)-intercept \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\) of Figure 9.5(a) becomes the \(y\)-intercept \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) of Figure 9.5(b), because \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\) gives \(\cos^{-1} 0 = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
The curve in Figure 9.5(b) goes downward from left to right: \(\cos^{-1} x\) is a decreasing function. A larger number has a smaller angle.

blocks.caption: Some values of the principal inverse cosine (our table; every value lies in [0, π])

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Look at the negative inputs in the table: they give obtuse angles. For example, \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) and not \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\), because negative angles are outside \([0, \pi]\).
A pattern you can see in the table: \(\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x\), e.g. \(\frac{2\pi}{3} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{3}\). It holds because \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\). (For sine the pattern is different: \(\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1} x\).)

The graph of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is also obtain by reflecting the graph of the principal cosine function \(y = \cos x\) along the line \(y = x\) as a mirror image, shown in Figure 9.6. Observe that the graph of \(y = \cos x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).
book_errors: Observe that the graph of \(y = \cos x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "is also obtain by reflecting"; it should be "is also obtained by reflecting". It also prints "Observe that the graph of \(y = \cos x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\)". The graph of \(y = \cos x\) alone is not symmetric about \(y = x\); the correct statement is that the graphs of \(y = \cos x\) (principal) and \(y = \cos^{-1} x\) are symmetric about the line \(y = x\) (mirror images of each other).

blocks.alt: The principal cosine curve from (0, 1) to (pi, minus 1) and the inverse cosine curve from (minus 1, pi) to (1, 0), drawn together with the dashed line y = x. Each curve is the mirror image of the other in that line.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.6: y = cos x and y = cos⁻¹ x are mirror images in the line y = x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In Figure 9.6 the two curves cross each other on the line \(y = x\), at the point where \(\cos x = x\) (about \(x \approx 0.739\)). A function and its inverse can only meet on the mirror line or in mirror pairs, never anywhere else at random.

Like the sine function, the cosine function with range \([-1, 1]\) can be restricted to any one of the infinitely many intervals \([-2\pi, -\pi]\), \([-\pi, 0]\), \([0, \pi]\), \([\pi, 2\pi]\), or generally \([n\pi, n\pi + \pi]\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), to make the cosine function one-to-one. If no interval is specified, then \(\cos^{-1} x\) is a function with domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \([0, \pi]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Each of these intervals has length \(\pi\) and runs from one maximum or minimum of cosine to the next one (see the dots in Figure 9.4), so cosine is strictly decreasing or strictly increasing on it. The standard choice is \(n = 0\), i.e. \([0, \pi]\); its values are the principal values.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\) is \(\sec x\). For example (ours), \(\cos^{-1} 0 = \frac{\pi}{2}\), while \(\frac{1}{\cos 0} = 1\). The \(-1\) in \(\cos^{-1}\) names the inverse function; it is not a power.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Principal cosine function: \(\cos : [0, \pi] \to [-1, 1]\), which is bijective.
2. \(y = \cos^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \cos y\), with domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \([0, \pi]\).
3. \(\cos^{-1}\) of a negative number is an obtuse angle in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\); never a negative angle.
4. The graph of \(y = \cos^{-1} x\) is the mirror image of the principal cosine graph in \(y = x\); it decreases from \((-1, \pi)\) to \((1, 0)\).
5. \(\cos^{-1} x\) is not \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using the sine range for cosine: \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\) is wrong; the answer is \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\).
2. Writing \(\cos^{-1} 1 = 2\pi\): \(2\pi\) is outside \([0, \pi]\); the answer is \(0\).
3. Applying \(\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1} x\) to cosine: for cosine the rule is \(\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x\).
4. Reading \(\cos^{-1} x\) as \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\).
